newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia energy minister resigns for private sector.
newsitem.headline: Russia energy minister resigns for private sector.

text.p: Russian Fuel and Energy Minister Pyotr Rodionov tendered his resignation on Friday, leaving a post that oversaw struggling domestic oil firms and stalled billion-dollar projects in a major world energy producer.
Fuel and Energy Ministry spokesman Sergei Slesaryev, who told Reuters of the resignation, would not comment on the reasons for Rodionov's decision to go.

No replacement has been announced and Slesaryev said the government press service would release a statement soon. Itar-Tass news agency said Rodionov would return to the private sector but did not say which company he would join.
Rodionov, appointed minister in August 1996, was previously director of Lentransgaz, the St Petersburg-based regional transport unit of Russian natural gas monopoly Gazprom.
As minister he had charge of the Russian economy's biggest export earners but faced a challenge in helping the oil sector, which has shown steep declines for a decade, to recover.
Russian oil output was 6.03 million barrels per day last year, down from a 1987 peak of 11.39 million barrels per day.
Russia, once the world's biggest oil producer, now ranks third behind Saudi Arabia and the United States.
Foreign oil and gas companies say they are ready to invest $50-70 billion in Russian energy projects, but Moscow has not yet passed the legislation needed to underpin the deals.
Recovery in the energy sector, which accounts for the bulk of tax revenues to the federal budget and a substantial chunk of gross domestic product, is key to Russian economic revival.

GDP has been contracting since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, although International Monetary Fund Managing Director Michel Camdessus said on Thursday that growth could start this year -- if Russian economic policies were right.

But the sector has changed dramatically in the years since the Soviet Union fell apart and Russian oil companies are now privatised, integrated and enthusiastically traded on a nascent stock market dominated by foreign cash.
Gazprom, the world's largest natural gas company, has remained a monopoly and has forged ahead with multi-billion-dollar plans to increase its already substantial gas exports.
The coal sector has seen some downsizing, while electricity plants may be restructured to bring competition into the sector.

Many of the best specialists in the Fuel and Energy Ministry have already left for the new private sector. Rodionov's predecessor Yuri Shafranik is now chairman of the board at the Tyumen Oil Company.
